messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Diego is a sixty-two-year-old dancer who has spent his life moving through space with precision, control, and grace. He came to therapy at the insistence of his wife, who had grown worried about the changes she saw in him over the past eight months—the way he flinched when she touched his shoulder, the nights he spent sitting upright in the living room until three in the morning, the distant look in his eyes that she could not reach. Diego himself was not sure what he hoped for. He only knew that something in him had broken, and he could not find a way back.

The event that broke him happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Diego was driving home from a rehearsal, his body still humming with the rhythm of the choreography he had just taught. He was stopped at a red light when a pickup truck ran the intersection at full speed and slammed into the driver’s side of his sedan. The impact spun the car twice before it came to rest against a lamppost. Diego remembers the sound of twisting metal, the shattering of glass, the sensation of his own body being thrown sideways against the seatbelt. He remembers the smell of gasoline and the sight of steam rising from the crumpled hood. He remembers, most vividly, the sound of the other driver’s radio still playing—a tinny pop song—as everything went silent around him. He was trapped in the car for nearly twenty minutes before emergency services cut him free. He sustained a fractured rib, a concussion, and deep bruising across his chest and arms. But what haunts him is not the physical pain. What haunts him is that he cannot put any of it into words. When he tries to tell someone what happened, the sentences dissolve. He can see the scene in his mind, hear the sounds, feel the pressure of the seatbelt against his chest, but the story itself will not form. He has come to believe that this failure to speak about it means something terrible about him—that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he is, someone weak, someone who deserved to be caught in that moment of helplessness. He is certain now that he cannot stop bad things from happening to him, and that he will never again feel normal emotions, only this flat, hollow dread that has taken up residence in his chest.

In the months following the crash, Diego’s life contracted slowly, then all at once. He stopped driving, which was manageable at first because his wife could take him to the studio. But the studio itself became a problem. The rehearsal space had only one entrance, and every time Diego walked in, he found himself scanning the walls for exits, counting doors, measuring the distance to the fire escape. He could not concentrate on the choreography. He would stand in the center of the floor and hear, in his head, the screech of metal and the pop song that had played from the other driver’s radio. The shame that rose with those memories was overwhelming—a hot, sickening feeling that made him want to disappear into his own body. He began to deliberately dissociate during rehearsals, trying to leave his own skin, to blank out the sounds and the images. He learned to make his mind go numb, to stare at a fixed point on the wall until everything went fuzzy. His teaching suffered. His students noticed that he was no longer present. He started canceling classes, then stopped going to the studio altogether.

At home, Diego found that the only way to avoid the memories was to stay awake until he was too exhausted to dream. He would sit in the dark living room, watching old dance videos on mute, until his wife went to bed. Then he would stay up another hour, sometimes two, until his eyes burned and his thoughts finally slowed. Sleep, when it came, was shallow and filled with fragments he could not control. He became hypervigilant to touch. If his wife placed a hand on his back while he was washing dishes, he would jump, his heart hammering, his fists clenching before he could stop himself. He knew it was unreasonable—she was only trying to comfort him—but he could not help the surge of alarm that overtook his body. He began to avoid her at certain times of day, positioning himself so that she could not approach him from behind. He started eating dinner standing up, facing the kitchen door, so that he could see anyone who entered.

What finally brought Diego to therapy was not his own suffering, but a single moment with his wife. She had come home from work, found him sitting in the dark again, and sat down across from him without touching him. She said, very quietly, “I don’t know who you are anymore.” Diego looked at her and realized that he did not know either. He was terrified that she was right, that the person he had been—the dancer, the teacher, the man who moved through the world with confidence—was gone forever. He came to the first session with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, unable to look the therapist in the eye. He said he wanted to feel something other than shame and fear. He said he wanted to stop being afraid of his own life. But underneath that, what he did not say aloud was that he was terrified he had already become the person the crash proved him to be, and that no amount of talking could change that.
